identification.summary: Calypso is an APT group first detected by Positive Technologies Expert Security Center in March 2019; PT assessed it as active since at least September 2016 and focused on stealing confidential data from state institutions [S1][S2]. PT judged the group likely to be of Asian origin; media coverage characterized it as Chinese-speaking [S1][S2][S3].
identification.firstObserved: Positive Technologies: active since at least September 2016; first detected March 2019 [S1][S2].
identification.notes: Existing record lists aliases BRONZE MEDLEY (Secureworks CTU) and Red Lamassu (PwC page URL in imported references); neither alias was confirmed from a fetched source in this pass. Recorded Future and Dr.Web describe overlap with PT/ESET reporting on Calypso [S4][S6]. ESET named Calypso among groups exploiting Exchange in March 2021 [S5].

attribution.confidence: Positive Technologies stated the group is likely of Asian origin; coverage of PT's report says it is Chinese-speaking based on PlugX and Byeby use and exposed IP addresses from Chinese providers [S1][S2][S3]. Recorded Future describes Calypso as a suspected Chinese state-sponsored group [S4]. No government attribution found.
attribution.basis: Tool overlap (PlugX, Byeby) and infrastructure artifacts per PT as relayed by media [S2][S3]; vendor characterization by Recorded Future [S4].

objectives: Theft of confidential data from government institutions per Positive Technologies [S1][S2]. Later reporting shows access to telecom and Exchange mail servers consistent with espionage [S4][S6].

regions: India, Brazil, Kazakhstan, Russia, Thailand, Turkey (PT 2019) [S1][S2]
Geographically widespread Exchange victims, including Australia and Czech Republic (Recorded Future, per search summary) [S4]
targeting.notes: PT's 2019 government-victim split reported by media: India 34%, Brazil 18%, Kazakhstan 18%, Russia 12%, Thailand 12%, Turkey 6% [S2][S3]. Recorded Future judged 2021 Exchange targeting likely opportunistic [S4].

capabilities.summary: Initial access via the Windows SMB vulnerability CVE-2017-0143 or stolen credentials; then the Calypso RAT/web shell for command execution and tool upload; also public tools such as SysInternals, Mimikatz, EternalBlue and EternalRomance [S2][S3]. PT reported Byeby trojan and PlugX use [S3]. In March 2021 the group was reported to exploit ProxyLogon Exchange flaws (CVE-2021-26855, CVE-2021-27065), deploy a web shell and load PlugX [S4][S5]. Dr.Web reported PlugX, Whitebird, Fast Reverse Proxy and RemCom in a Kazakh telecom intrusion dating from 2019, and a C2 panel called Remote Rover [S6].

campaigns.name: Earliest PT-observed activity
campaigns.summary: PT assessed the group active since at least September 2016 [S1][S2].

campaigns.name: Discovery by Positive Technologies
campaigns.summary: PT detected the group and identified victims and control servers; targets were state institutions in six countries [S1][S2].

campaigns.name: Public disclosure of Calypso campaign
campaigns.summary: PT publicly reported the campaign against government bodies in Brazil, India, Kazakhstan, Russia, Thailand and Turkey [S2][S3].

campaigns.name: Exchange ProxyLogon exploitation
campaigns.summary: ESET listed Calypso among groups exploiting Exchange flaws; Recorded Future reported a surge from 1 March 2021 in victim traffic to PlugX C2 infrastructure attributed to Calypso and noted the C2 IP was first flagged in November 2020 [S4][S5].

campaigns.name: Dr.Web report on Kazakh telecom intrusion
campaigns.summary: Dr.Web, contacted in October 2021, found servers compromised since 2019 and attributed the activity to Calypso by tools, methods and infrastructure [S6].

diamond.adversary: Suspected Asian-origin group (described by media and Recorded Future as Chinese); sponsor not established [S1][S3][S4].
diamond.capability: SMB exploit or stolen credentials, Calypso RAT/web shell, PlugX, Byeby, Whitebird, Mimikatz, ProxyLogon exploitation [S2][S3][S4][S6].
diamond.infrastructure: Control servers identified by PT; PlugX C2 IP 91.220.203.86 flagged by Recorded Future; Remote Rover C2 panel per Dr.Web [S1][S4][S6].
diamond.victim: Government institutions, a Kazakh telecom, and Exchange-hosting organizations worldwide [S2][S4][S6].
diamond.technology: Unpatched SMB services, internet-exposed Exchange servers, and weak credential hygiene [S2][S4].

gaps: No government attribution or named sponsor was found.

Primary documents could not be opened (fetch failed): PT report, PwC Red Lamassu page, Recorded Future, ESET and Dr.Web originals. Content relied on search-result summaries and press coverage of PT [S2][S3].
The PwC Red Lamassu report (referenced in imported data) could not be dated or read, so the Red Lamassu alias and a reported open-directory/JFM backdoor analysis are unverified.
BRONZE MEDLEY (Secureworks) alias not verified from a source in this pass.
MITRE ATT&CK has no group id in the record; overlap with other Chinese clusters using PlugX is not resolved.
Microsoft's name for this actor, if any, is not established.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Internet-exposed Exchange servers, SMB services and telecom mail infrastructure are key terrain. STEP 2: The actor weaponizes freshly disclosed Exchange flaws within days and reuses long-lived PlugX infrastructure [S4][S5]. STEP 3: Template is SMB or credential access or Exchange exploit, then web shell, PlugX/Whitebird, credential dumping, lateral movement with RemCom and FRP [S2][S6]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued data theft from government and telecom networks in South/Central Asia and beyond. MDCOA is opportunistic mass Exchange exploitation reaching defense-adjacent or coalition partner mail systems. Candidate indicators: unexpected web shells on Exchange, PlugX beaconing to known C2 IPs, RemCom and Fast Reverse Proxy binaries on domain controllers [S4][S6].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track Exchange and SMB patch status for partner and DoD-adjacent networks, since exploitation is opportunistic [S4]. (2) Authorities: coordinate partner-network hunts through established defensive channels; the actor is not tied to a government sponsor in the sources. (3) Mission assurance: prioritize telecom and mail-server dependencies that attackers held for years undetected [S6]. (4) Coordination: share IOC sets from PT, Recorded Future and Dr.Web with DC3 and allied CERTs.
